title: Tenant Request Routing Board
note: Spec/data file for the artifact described in ARTIFACT-BRIEF.md. This is structured content only — no HTML/JS is implemented here. All caller lines are constructed illustrations of call types, never a transcript of a real tenant call, and never attributed to Weissmann or any named competitor as a measured result.

routine.label: Routine — administrative queue
routine.description: No time pressure. The assistant listens, categorises, and routes or schedules — the same job as filing correctly.
routine.aiRole: Handles the full interaction: captures the details, confirms next steps, logs the request.
routine.humanRole: Reviewed on the normal schedule; no immediate involvement required.
routine.typicalResponseTime: Standard queue — next available slot, no fixed deadline.

urgent.label: Urgent — fast-tracked, still administrative
urgent.description: Not a danger signal, but leaving it in the standard queue creates real hardship. The assistant still is not judging risk here — it is applying a fixed priority rule to a known category.
urgent.aiRole: Captures the details, flags the request as high priority, and notifies the relevant contractor or caretaker the same day.
urgent.humanRole: Acts within a defined short window (typically same business day) rather than the standard queue.

emergency.label: Emergency — immediate human escalation
emergency.description: The assistant never evaluates how dangerous the situation actually is. Recognising one of a small, fixed set of signal words is enough on its own — escalation is immediate and automatic, not a judgement call, and confidence or calmness in the caller's voice does not change it.
emergency.aiRole: Does not gather the usual intake details first. Connects the caller to a human immediately, or gives them the direct emergency number if nobody can be reached instantly. Logs the call as flagged afterwards.
emergency.humanRole: Assesses the actual danger and decides what happens next — the human, not the AI, makes the safety judgement.

alwaysEscalateTriggers: Smell of gas, or any suspicion of a gas leak
Active flooding or a burst pipe (water currently spreading, not a slow drip)
Smoke, or any indication of fire
Signs of a break-in, forced entry, or an intruder on the property
Any mention of injury or of someone's safety being at risk right now

scenarios.label: Dripping tap
scenarios.callerLine: There's a tap in the bathroom that's been dripping since Tuesday. It's not urgent, just annoying.
scenarios.aiAction: Logs the request, confirms the unit and the exact tap location, and adds it to the standard maintenance queue.
scenarios.humanInvolvement: Reviewed on the normal schedule — no same-day action required.
scenarios.note: A slow, contained drip is exactly the kind of call an AI system should handle from start to finish without involving anyone immediately.

scenarios.label: No heat in winter
scenarios.callerLine: The heating hasn't worked since yesterday morning and it's minus two outside.
scenarios.aiAction: Logs the request as high priority, notifies the heating contractor the same day, and tells the tenant when to expect contact.
scenarios.humanInvolvement: Acted on within the same business day — not the standard queue, but not an emergency transfer either.
scenarios.note: Nobody is in danger the way a gas leak implies danger, but a cold home for several days is a real hardship. This gets fast-tracked, not escalated as an emergency.

scenarios.label: Lost key
scenarios.callerLine: I've lost my key somewhere between the office and home — can I get a replacement?
scenarios.aiAction: Logs the request and explains the standard replacement or spare-key process.
scenarios.humanInvolvement: Handled through the normal replacement process; no immediate action needed.
scenarios.note: A lost key during ordinary hours is paperwork, not a crisis. It would only move to a different category if the caller were currently locked out with no fallback available.

scenarios.label: Noise complaint
scenarios.callerLine: The neighbours upstairs have had loud music going since eleven, and it's not the first time.
scenarios.aiAction: Logs the complaint, the unit involved, and how often it has happened, then routes it to the property manager for a decision.
scenarios.humanInvolvement: A person reviews and decides how to handle it — not resolved on the call.
scenarios.note: This needs a value judgement about who is right and what to do next. The assistant's job stops at listening accurately and filing correctly.

scenarios.label: Viewing request
scenarios.callerLine: I saw the listing for the two-bedroom on Bahnhofstrasse — could I arrange a viewing this week?
scenarios.aiAction: Checks available slots and books the viewing directly, or proposes alternatives if none are open this week.
scenarios.humanInvolvement: None required unless the caller has a request outside the standard process.
scenarios.note: A booking action with no danger dimension at all — the clearest possible case for full automation.

scenarios.label: Rent document request
scenarios.callerLine: I need a copy of my rent statement for this year for my tax return.
scenarios.aiAction: Confirms the identity details already on file and arranges for the document to be sent.
scenarios.humanInvolvement: Sent through the standard document process; no urgency attached.
scenarios.note: Paperwork, not a problem — logged and routed like any other administrative request.

scenarios.label: Smell of gas
scenarios.callerLine: I think I can smell gas near the kitchen — I'm not totally sure.
scenarios.aiAction: Does not ask for the unit number or run through normal intake questions first. Connects the caller to a human immediately, or gives the direct emergency number if nobody is reached within seconds. Logs the call as flagged afterwards.
scenarios.humanInvolvement: A person assesses the situation immediately — the danger judgement is made by a human, not inferred by the AI from how calm or unsure the caller sounds.
scenarios.note: "I'm not totally sure" does not downgrade this call. The trigger is the word "gas," not the caller's confidence.

scenarios.label: Active flooding / burst pipe
scenarios.callerLine: Water is coming out from under the sink — it's already on the floor and spreading.
scenarios.aiAction: Escalates immediately, the same way as the gas-smell scenario — no diagnostic questions about the pipe or the damage first.
scenarios.humanInvolvement: A person coordinates an emergency plumber and, if needed, other affected units — decisions the AI does not make.
scenarios.note: The distinction from the dripping-tap scenario is not the word "water" — it's "spreading" versus "since Tuesday." Both matter for accurate routing; only one requires immediate escalation.

scenarios.label: Break-in / forced entry
scenarios.callerLine: My door looks like it's been forced open. I don't think anyone's inside right now, but I haven't gone in.
scenarios.aiAction: Escalates immediately and, depending on configuration, advises the caller not to enter the unit while connecting them to a human or the police.
scenarios.humanInvolvement: A person, and where relevant the police, take over entirely — well outside anything an administrative system should attempt to manage.
scenarios.note: The caller's own uncertainty ("I don't think anyone's inside") is exactly why this cannot be left to a script — it goes straight to a human.

scenarios.label: Smoke or signs of fire
scenarios.callerLine: There's smoke coming from the stairwell on the third floor.
scenarios.aiAction: Escalates immediately and, if nobody can be reached instantly, tells the caller to contact the fire brigade directly rather than waiting on the line.
scenarios.humanInvolvement: Emergency services and the property manager decide what happens next — not the AI.
scenarios.note: Speed matters more than internal process here. The assistant does not try to route this through the normal escalation chain first.

uiRules.noSeverityScoring: This tool must never compute, display, or imply that the AI measured or ranked how dangerous a scenario is (e.g. no '78% risk' or similar). It only shows the fixed category a scenario belongs to and the fixed rule attached to that category.
uiRules.colorRule: Never use colour alone to distinguish Routine / Urgent / Emergency — always pair with the text label. Emergency should read clearly as text even to a user with no colour perception.
uiRules.emergencyFraming: For emergency scenarios, the UI copy must always say the AI 'recognised a fixed signal' and 'escalated immediately' — never that it 'decided,' 'judged,' 'assessed,' or 'determined' the situation was dangerous. That judgement belongs to the human it hands over to.
uiRules.noDefaultSelection: No scenario is pre-selected on load — the board starts empty with a prompt to choose a call type, so the tool never implies a single 'typical' call.

primary.label: Test how the escalation rules would actually work (CHF 350, one-time)

secondary.label: Read the full article on triage vs. emergency judgement
secondary.hrefNote: Links to the academy spoke page for the ai-phone-assistant-property-management article.

disclaimerText: All caller lines in this tool are constructed illustrations of common call types, not recordings or transcripts of a real tenant call, and not a measured result from Weissmann or any other vendor's system. The routing shown is an example of good triage design, not a documented specification of any single product.
privacyNote: This tool runs entirely in the browser. There is no field for a real name, address, phone number, or apartment number at any point — it only displays fixed example scenarios and reflects back which one you selected, without transmitting or storing anything.
